  Redrawing and saving heatmaps, extracting their orders and clusters, tidy
  data for ggplot2, heatmaps beside ggplot2 plots and alternative text for
  screen readers.
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 7,
  out.width = "100%",
  fig.align = "center"
)
```

`heat_map()` draws a heatmap and returns it as an object. This article shows what you can do with that object: redraw it with changes, save it, take its orders and clusters for further analysis, rebuild it in `ggplot2`, place it beside `ggplot2` plots, and describe it in words for readers who can't see it.

```{r first, fig.alt = "The mtcars heatmap with each column converted to z-scores, the cars and variables clustered by dendrograms and the cars cut into three groups labelled A, B and C."}
library(HeatmapR)
hm <- heat_map(
  mtcars,
  scale = "zscore",
  tree = "both",
  tree_cut_y = 3,
  tree_label_y = TRUE,
  tree_label_text_y = c("A", "B", "C"),
  legend_title = "z-score",
  title = "mtcars"
)
```

## Redrawing and saving

A `heat_map` object is the `recordedplot` of the heatmap together with the arguments that made it. `print()` and `plot()` draw it again, with any argument replaced, and `data` draws other data with the same settings. The slow steps (dendrograms, k-means clusters, branch support) are reused when nothing they depend on has changed, so a redraw only draws.

```{r redraw, fig.alt = "The same z-scored mtcars heatmap redrawn with circles sized by the absolute z-score and a new title, with the same dendrograms and the three groups of cars labelled A, B and C."}
plot(hm, cell_shape = "circle", cell_size = abs(scale(mtcars)),
     title = "mtcars, redrawn")
```

`heat_map_save()` writes a heatmap to a file (PNG, JPEG, TIFF, PDF or SVG, from the extension), at the size and resolution you choose: either the object itself (`x = hm`) or every heatmap drawn after the call until `heat_map_complete()`.

```{r save}
file <- tempfile(fileext = ".pdf")
heat_map_save(file, x = hm, width = 6, height = 7)
file.exists(file)
```

## Orders, clusters and colours

`heat_map_info()` returns what the heatmap is made of: the data as displayed (after scaling), the order of the rows and columns, the cluster of each row and column, the dendrograms, the colour, size and shape of every cell, and the bounding box of every component in inches.

```{r info}
info <- heat_map_info(hm)
names(info)
# THE ROWS IN THE ORDER THEY ARE SHOWN, FROM THE TOP
head(rownames(mtcars)[info$row_order])
# THE CLUSTER OF EACH CAR
split(rownames(mtcars), info$row_clusters)
info$layout[1:4, ]
```

The clusters are numbered from the top of the heatmap, as they are labelled, so they can be used straight away, e.g. to compare the cars of each cluster:

```{r clusters}
aggregate(mtcars[, c("mpg", "hp", "wt")], list(cluster = info$row_clusters), mean)
```

## Tidy data for ggplot2

`heat_map_data()` returns what the heatmap shows as tidy tables: one row per cell, row, column or dendrogram segment. `x` and `y` are the centres of the cells in the heatmap's own co-ordinates, including the gaps between clusters, so a heatmap can be rebuilt or restyled with `ggplot2`, exported, or drawn on with base graphics.

```{r data}
cells <- heat_map_data(hm)
head(cells)
```

```{r ggplot, fig.alt = "A ggplot2 version of the mtcars heatmap built from the tidy data: tiles in the heatmap's order and grouping on a red-blue scale, with the row dendrogram drawn as segments to the right of the tiles."}
library(ggplot2)
rows <- heat_map_data(hm, "rows")
cols <- heat_map_data(hm, "columns")
tree <- heat_map_data(hm, "tree_y")
edge <- max(cells$x) + 0.5
grow <- function(h) edge + 3 * h / max(tree$x)
ggplot(cells) +
  geom_tile(aes(x, y, fill = value), colour = "white") +
  geom_segment(data = tree, aes(x = grow(x), y = y, xend = grow(xend), yend = yend)) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "RdBu", name = "z-score") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = cols$x, labels = cols$column) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = rows$y, labels = rows$row) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5))
```

Drawn straight after `heat_map()`, base graphics land on the cells. Below, the largest value in each column is marked with a star:

```{r points, fig.alt = "The z-scored mtcars heatmap with a white star on the cell holding the highest value of each column."}
hm <- heat_map(mtcars, scale = "zscore", tree = "both", legend_title = "z-score")
cells <- heat_map_data(hm)
top <- cells[ave(cells$value, cells$column, FUN = max) == cells$value, ]
points(top$x, top$y, pch = 8, col = "white", cex = 1.5)
```

## Beside ggplot2 plots

`heat_map_grob()` turns a heatmap into a `grid` graphical object, so it can sit beside `ggplot2` plots in `patchwork`, `cowplot` or `gridExtra` layouts. The grob draws the heatmap again whenever its space changes, so dendrograms, legends and text are sized for the space it is given. It needs the **gridGraphics** package.

```{r patchwork, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "A scatter plot of miles per gallon against weight for the mtcars cars coloured by number of cylinders, on the left, beside the clustered mtcars heatmap on the right, arranged with patchwork."}
library(patchwork)
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Weight (1000 lbs)", y = "Miles per gallon", colour = "Cylinders") +
  theme_bw()
p + heat_map_grob(hm, title = "mtcars") + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.5))
```

Several heatmaps can also share one figure with `heat_map_custom()`, which takes a layout (a number of rows and columns, or a matrix as in `graphics::layout()`), and `heat_map_complete()` to finish it.

```{r layout, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "Three heatmaps side by side, one each for the Mercedes cars, the Mazda and Toyota cars, and the Hornet, Datsun and Volvo cars, each with its own title."}
heat_map_custom(popup = FALSE, layout = c(1, 3))
heat_map(mtcars[grepl("Merc", rownames(mtcars)), ], scale = "column",
         legend = FALSE, title = "Mercedes")
heat_map(mtcars[grepl("Mazda|Toyota", rownames(mtcars)), ], scale = "column",
         legend = FALSE, title = "Mazda | Toyota")
heat_map(mtcars[grepl("Hornet|Datsun|Volvo", rownames(mtcars)), ],
         scale = "column", legend = FALSE, title = "Hornet | Datsun | Volvo")
heat_map_complete()
```

Heatmaps drawn on their own each have their own colour scale, so one colour can stand for different values in each. `heat_map_arrange()` redraws heatmaps in one layout on shared colour limits (and cell size limits), from the lowest to the highest limit of them all, and keeps their dendrograms and other settings:

```{r arrange-make, fig.show = "hide"}
merc <- heat_map(mtcars[grepl("Merc", rownames(mtcars)), ], title = "Mercedes")
others <- heat_map(mtcars[!grepl("Merc", rownames(mtcars)), ],
                   title = "The other cars")
```

```{r arrange, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Two heatmaps of the unscaled mtcars values side by side, the 7 Mercedes cars and the 25 other cars, both on one colour scale from 0 to 472, so the displacement of the Mercedes cars, at most 276, is teal to yellow while that of the largest American cars reaches dark red."}
heat_map_arrange(merc, others)
```

## Alternative text

Figures in reports and on the web need alternative text for readers using screen readers, and a heatmap is hard to describe by hand. `heat_map_describe()` writes the description from the heatmap itself: its size and scaling, what the colours show (naming the colours of the scale), the most extreme values, how the rows and columns are ordered, and where each cluster is highest and lowest, plus branch support, uncertainty, annotations, bars and zoom panels when the heatmap has them.

```{r describe, fig.show = "hide"}
hm <- heat_map(mtcars, scale = "zscore", tree = "both", tree_cut_y = 3,
               legend_title = "z-score", title = "mtcars")
heat_map_describe(hm)
```

In R Markdown and Quarto the description can be the figure's alternative text: draw the heatmap in one chunk and pass the description to the `fig.alt` option of the chunk that shows it.

````markdown
```{r, include = FALSE}`r ''`
hm <- heat_map(mtcars, scale = "zscore", tree = "both", tree_cut_y = 3)
```

```{r, fig.alt = heat_map_describe(hm)}`r ''`
hm
```
````

```{r alt, include = FALSE}
hm <- heat_map(mtcars, scale = "zscore", tree = "both", tree_cut_y = 3,
               legend_title = "z-score", title = "Described by heat_map_describe()")
```

```{r alt-show, fig.alt = as.character(heat_map_describe(hm))}
hm
```

## Colour-blind readers

About one man in twelve of northern European descent has a red-green colour-vision deficiency. `heat_map_check_colours()` simulates how a heatmap's colours look with deuteranopia, protanopia and tritanopia (as Machado et al. 2009 model them) and lists the annotation levels, values of non-numeric cells, stacked bar parts and branch colours that become hard to tell apart, and colour scales whose distant values end up looking alike. Here matplotlib's red and green, which most readers tell apart easily, are close for readers with deuteranopia:

```{r colour-check, fig.show = "hide"}
cylinders <- data.frame(cylinders = factor(mtcars$cyl), row.names = rownames(mtcars))
hm <- heat_map(mtcars, scale = "column", annotation_y = cylinders,
               annotation_colours = list(cylinders = c("#D62728", "#2CA02C", "#1F77B4")))
heat_map_check_colours(hm)
```

`options(HeatmapR.check_colours = TRUE)` checks every heatmap as it is drawn, with a message when colours are hard to tell apart. The first eight colours of `palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito")` stay apart for each deficiency, and the default colour scale changes in lightness from end to end, so its values stay readable.
